question:
Patient note:
A 24-year-old man who works part-time as a computer-graphics intern while completing an online bachelor’s degree in digital design was referred to the medical center’s combined pulmonary–hepatology clinic this morning for an updated assessment before his university health-insurance board considers financing a listing evaluation at the regional transplant program. He was diagnosed in infancy with a multisystem genetic condition characterized by thick airway secretions, and over childhood he required multiple courses of intravenous antibiotics for bronchiectasis-related exacerbations; the most recent admission was nine months ago, and he has avoided hospitalization since then by performing twice-daily high-frequency chest-wall oscillation, using nebulized hypertonic saline and dornase alfa, and adhering to a dual-bronchodilator regimen consisting of tiotropium inhalation each dawn and a budesonide–formoterol dry-powder device twice daily. Spirometry obtained four weeks ago by his local pulmonologist documented an FEV1 of 1.15 L (38 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.46 and less than 4 % bronchodilator reversibility, findings that have been stable for the past year; resting oxygen saturation today is 94 % on room air and falls to 89 % after a seven-minute walk that he finishes with a respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min, though he has never required long-term supplemental oxygen or non-invasive ventilation. He denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, pedal edema, exertional chest pressure, or palpitations, and a transthoracic echocardiogram performed six months earlier in the context of progressive fatigue revealed normal right- and left-sided chamber dimensions with an ejection fraction of 65 %, no regional wall-motion abnormality, and an estimated pulmonary-artery systolic pressure of 28 mm Hg. Vascular history is unremarkable: he bikes three miles to class when weather allows without calf cramping, ankle–brachial indices measured for a research registry last year were 1.02 bilaterally, and distal pulses today are 2+ symmetrically. Neurologic review discloses no episodes of slurred speech, unilateral weakness, or transient visual loss; he codes complex animation sequences without difficulty and scored 30/30 on a Montreal Cognitive Assessment administered last semester as part of a psychology elective. Endocrine notes indicate that two years ago routine surveillance labs revealed fasting plasma glucose 168 mg/dL and a glycated hemoglobin of 7.8 %; since then he has used a basal-bolus insulin program (glargine 14 units at bedtime, lispro carb-matched) with self-monitored morning readings ranging 90–165 mg/dL and most recent A1c 7.4 %. He has no sensory loss to monofilament at the great toes, retinal photography six months ago showed only occasional microaneurysms without macular thickening, and a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio remains below 20 mg/g. Renal indices are otherwise normal—serum creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate 120 mL/min/1.73 m², blood urea nitrogen 11 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, and urinalysis bland. The major systemic burden lies in the hepatobiliary tract: abdominal ultrasound three weeks ago showed a nodular, heterogeneous 18-cm liver with coarse echotexture, splenic length 18 cm, mild ascites in the perisplenic recess, and patent portal and hepatic veins; transient elastography recorded a median stiffness of 21 kPa. Laboratory chemistry this morning lists alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 66 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 245 U/L, total bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL, direct fraction 0.9 mg/dL, albumin 2.9 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.5. Platelet count is 85 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, and white-blood-cell count 6.1 × 10⁹/L. He reports a single episode of hematemesis thirteen months ago treated with endoscopic variceal ligation, and since then he has taken nadolol 20 mg nightly; he also maintains a low-sodium diet and uses furosemide 20 mg with spironolactone 50 mg each morning for trace ankle swelling that develops if his weight increases by more than 1 kg. He has never manifested confusion suggestive of overt encephalopathy, though a standing prescription for lactulose syrup is filled and kept at home. Gastrointestinal review notes good appetite but early satiety, no abdominal pain, melena, or jaundice beyond a faint scleral icterus observable today. He denies fevers, chills, night sweats, or unintended weight loss, has never undergone chemotherapy or radiation, and no masses have been detected on serial imaging. Family history reveals a sibling with the same genetic lung disorder and early cirrhosis but no premature coronary events, strokes, or peripheral arterial procedures; there is no lineage of autoimmune rheumatologic illness. He never smoked, drinks only non-alcoholic beer at esports gatherings, and does not use recreational drugs. Current outpatient medications include pancreatic enzyme capsules with meals, vitamins A 4,000 IU and E 400 IU daily, ursodiol 600 mg twice daily, the inhaled agents mentioned, insulin as outlined, nadolol, spironolactone, furosemide, and a cholecalciferol supplement; he recalls a generalized urticarial rash after trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole at age 10 and avoids that antibiotic class. Vital signs at 09:15 record temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 102/60 mm Hg seated right arm, heart rate 88 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 94 % on ambient air; weight is 60 kg, height 175 cm, yielding a body-mass index of 19.6 kg/m². He appears thin but alert, converses in full sentences between occasional soft coughs producing scant mucoid sputum, and sits comfortably leaning slightly forward. Conjunctivae are pink with trace yellowing of the sclerae; neck veins rise 2 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, and there are no cervical bruits. Cardiac examination reveals a nondisplaced point of maximal impulse, crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are hyper-resonant to percussion; auscultation detects markedly prolonged expiration with scattered coarse crackles at both bases and faint end-expiratory wheezes. The abdomen is distended mildly, flank dullness shifts with position, and a firm nodular liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin while the spleen tip descends on inspiration. There is no guarding or rebound, bowel sounds are active, and a small umbilical hernia is reducible. Extremities show fine digital clubbing, trace bilateral ankle edema, and warm skin with good capillary refill; no spider telangiectasias are present. Neurologic screening demonstrates orientation to person, place, and date, fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, symmetric 5/5 strength throughout, and normal heel-to-shin coordination; tandem gait is limited by dyspnea rather than imbalance. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained in clinic displays normal sinus rhythm at 86 beats/min, PR interval 150 ms, QRS 90 ms, axis 20°, and no ST-segment displacement or pathologic Q waves. Portable posteroanterior chest radiograph shows hyperinflated lungs with scattered bronchial wall thickening, flattened diaphragms, and mild basilar infiltrative change but no cardiomegaly. He requests guidance on the timing of live-virus immunizations, optimization of calorie-dense nutrition to prevent further weight loss, and clarification of next steps toward combined lung–liver transplantation should his current functional status decline.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums age points and weighted comorbidities, counting only the highest applicable tier for each condition.
- Age 24 (<50): 0 points.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: bronchiectasis with persistent airflow obstruction (FEV1 38% predicted) and daily inhaled therapy: 1 point.
- Diabetes requiring insulin: no nephropathy, neuropathy, or proliferative retinopathy is documented. Occasional retinal microaneurysms alone do not meet the higher CCI end-organ damage criterion: 1 point.
- Moderate/severe liver disease: cirrhosis with portal hypertension, evidenced by prior variceal bleeding and ascites: 3 points. Do not also score mild liver disease.
- No other qualifying comorbidity: 0 points.
Total = 0 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 5.
Final answer: 5
